summary:
I developed the NASA Terrestrial Analog Finder, an interactive GIS dashboard and analysis toolkit for identifying Earth locations that resemble specific lunar and Martian environments. Users can select targets such as the lunar South Pole, lava tubes, Jezero Crater, or Elysium Planitia, then compare candidate analogs using adjustable weights for terrain, mineralogy, temperature, and surface roughness. Spectral and elevation visualizations, ranked matches, and printable mission dossiers help turn comparisons into practical field-testing plans.

The project addresses the challenge of finding terrestrial analogs by bringing satellite-informed data and quantitative, multi-criteria comparisons into one accessible tool, rather than relying only on familiar sites or qualitative judgments. Better-matched analogs can help researchers and mission teams test equipment, mobility, and field procedures on Earth—supporting safer, better-informed exploration while reducing the cost and risk of testing in space.
details:
Project overview

The Terrestrial Analog Finder is a decision-support tool for finding places on Earth with characteristics similar to specific lunar and Martian environments. Researchers select a target—such as the lunar South Pole, a lunar lava tube, Jezero Crater, or Elysium Planitia—and compare it with terrestrial candidate sites.

How it works

The platform ranks candidates using a weighted similarity score across four factors: topography, mineralogy, temperature, and surface roughness. Users can adjust the weights or choose a mission preset to see how priorities affect the rankings. The dashboard also provides map-based comparisons, elevation transects, spectral profiles, candidate match details, CSV export, and a printable Field Mission Dossier.

The project includes a browser-based interface using curated target and candidate data, plus a Python analysis pipeline for similarity scoring, batch comparisons, sensitivity testing, and searching for satellite products through NASA’s CMR and STAC interfaces. The analysis is designed around open observations such as lunar and Martian orbiter data and Earth datasets from sources including Copernicus, USGS, Sentinel-2, and ASTER.

Benefits and intended impact

The tool can help mission teams identify more relevant Earth sites for testing rover mobility, drills, instruments, and field procedures. Better-matched testing environments could improve preparation and reduce the cost and risk of discovering terrain or material challenges during a mission. Its rankings are intended for initial screening and planning, not as a substitute for validating data or conducting field research.

Tools and creative approach

The project uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interactive web application, including Leaflet mapping and Canvas visualizations; JSON for data and mission profiles; and Python for the analytical tools. No specialized hardware is required.

Its creative element is the combination of Earth and planetary observations in one adjustable workflow: instead of relying only on well-known analog locations, users can compare candidates against the specific conditions of a mission target. The project considers terrain, slope, roughness, spectral and mineral similarities, thermal conditions, mission objectives, and how sensitive results are to changes in user priorities.
